results.result: Larval body weight increases linearly from 3.0 to 4.0 days AEL, followed by a 12-hour period of slower growth, then remains constant. Weight stabilization at 4.5 days AEL coincides with cessation of feeding and the non-feeding stage, and weight remains constant through the WPP and WPP+1 stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are well-supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B and 1C. The temporal correlation between growth cessation and feeding cessation (C27) is further supported by citation to previous work on larval feeding behavior. The data clearly demonstrate the described growth trajectory.

results.result: Wing pouch volume increases linearly during the early-to-late third instar stage, continues to grow during the non-feeding larval stage, and ceases growth at the WPP stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by volumetric measurements in Figures 1D and 1E. The cessation of growth at WPP (C31) is further confirmed by PHH3 staining data showing the absence of dividing cells except in sensory organ precursor zones (C32-C33).

results.result: At the third instar larval stage, dividing cells are distributed throughout the wing pouch, whereas at the WPP stage, dividing cells are restricted to a narrow zone where sensory organ precursor cells divide.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are supported by PHH3 staining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-D and citation to previous work (Nolo et al., 2000). The spatial restriction of cell division at WPP is consistent with the cessation of wing pouch growth.

results.result: The hinge/notum domain shows similar linear-like growth trajectory as the wing pouch during early-to-late third instar, but stops growing during the non-feeding stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by experimental measurements in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and B. The differential timing of growth cessation between hinge/notum and wing pouch suggests distinct growth control mechanisms.

results.result: Allometric growth of the Drosophila wing pouch exhibits two phases of positive allometry, with an inflection point at the time when larvae cease feeding. The notum-hinge shows similar biphasic allometry but with more limited second-phase growth, suggesting multiple mechanisms control allometric growth of the wing imaginal disc.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by allometric growth data in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 5C. The biphasic pattern and differential behavior between wing pouch and notum-hinge provide strong evidence for multiple control mechanisms. The inference about multiple mechanisms (C45) is reasonable given the observed complexity.

results.result: Ds-GFP exhibits graded distribution along both AP and DV axes of the wing pouch, with high levels near the pouch border and low levels at the center. The gradient is asymmetric along the AP axis and becomes progressively shallower as the pouch grows. When normalized to pouch size, AP axis profiles collapse together, while DV axis profiles remain distinct due to progressive diminishment of both maximum and minimum Ds-GFP limits.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C55 are well-supported by fluorescence measurements in Figures 2C-F. The normalization analysis provides strong evidence for scaling behavior along the AP axis but not the DV axis. The data quality and consistency across developmental stages support these conclusions.

results.result: Fat-GFP exhibits a graded distribution opposite to Ds-GFP, with low levels near the pouch border and high levels at the center. The Fat gradient becomes progressively shallower and flattens along the AP axis at the WPP stage. When normalized to pouch size, Fat-GFP profiles do not collapse, with the minimum limit conserved but the maximum limit progressively diminishing as the wing pouch grows.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 are supported by fluorescence measurements in Figures 2G-J. The complementary gradient pattern to Ds-GFP and the distinct normalization behavior provide strong evidence. The flattening at WPP stage is clearly demonstrated in the data.

results.result: The graded distribution of Fat protein is generated by a post-transcriptional mechanism, as uniform fat gene transcription (confirmed by smFISH) produces a graded protein distribution, and Fat protein expressed under UAS-da-Gal4 control shows a similar gradient pattern to endogenous Fat.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by smFISH data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), citation to previous work, and the da-Gal4 experiment (Figure 2L). The logic is sound: uniform transcription producing graded protein distribution indicates post-transcriptional regulation. The da-Gal4 experiment provides strong confirmatory evidence.

results.result: The distribution of Fat and Ds proteins and wing pouch volume are unchanged in fj mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by fluorescence and volume measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-E. This negative result is important for ruling out Fj as the mechanism generating the Fat gradient.

results.result: In ds mutants, Fat-GFP levels at the wing pouch center are identical to wildtype, but levels near the pouch border are abnormally high, creating a more shallow gradient. The Fat-GFP profile does not flatten at the WPP stage but remains weakly graded, flattening somewhat more by WPP+1 stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by fluorescence measurements in Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B. The consistency with previous observations by Ma et al., 2003 (C70) strengthens the conclusion. The data clearly show the effect of Ds loss on Fat distribution.

results.result: Knockdown of perlecan (trol RNAi) reduces wing pouch area and increases thickness at the WPP stage, but has no effect on wing pouch volume or the Ds-GFP gradient. The Fat gradient flattens normally at the WPP stage. This demonstrates that Ds scales with wing pouch volume rather than area.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 are supported by measurements in Figures 3A-E. The experimental design is clever: by altering pouch dimensions while maintaining volume, the authors demonstrate volume-scaling of the Ds gradient. The inference (C76) is well-justified by the data.

results.result: Overexpression of RBF in the posterior compartment produces half the number of cells that are twofold larger, with unchanged compartment size. The Ds and Fat gradients in the P compartment are indistinguishable from wildtype at the WPP stage. This demonstrates that Ds and Fat gradient dynamics scale with wing pouch volume rather than cell number or area, indicating coupling to a global physical feature of the wing.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 are supported by data in Figures 3F-I and citation to previous work. The experimental design complements the trol(RNAi) experiment by altering cell number while maintaining volume. The inference about coupling to a global physical feature (C83) is well-supported by the combined evidence from both experiments.

results.result: Loss-of-function fat mutants delay the larva-pupa transition and overgrow the wing disc. Mutant larvae continue to increase in weight beyond the wildtype plateau until entering the non-feeding stage. The mutant larval notum and wing pouch grow at a faster rate than normal, and the wing pouch continues to grow at the larva-pupa transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by weight and growth measurements in Figures 4A-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B, along with citation to previous work. The data clearly demonstrate the overgrowth phenotype and altered developmental timing in fat mutants.

results.result: Loss-of-function ds mutants delay the larva-pupa transition by 12 hours. Mutant larvae continue to gain weight past the wildtype plateau until the larva-pupa transition. The mutant larval notum and wing pouch grow at a rate comparable to wildtype, but their growth period is extended. The notum ceases growth prior to the larva-pupa transition, but the wing pouch only stops growing at the WPP+1 stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 are supported by weight and growth measurements in Figures 4A-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B. The ds mutant phenotype differs from fat mutants in showing extended growth period rather than increased growth rate, suggesting distinct mechanisms.

results.result: Allometric growth of fat and ds mutant wing pouches is significantly different from wildtype, with a first phase more extended than normal and a second phase less extended than normal. Similar trends are observed for the notum in these mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are supported by allometric growth data in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C. The altered allometric relationships demonstrate that Fat and Ds regulate the relative scaling of wing growth to body growth.

results.result: RNAi against ds in the wing pouch results in near-complete depletion of Ds protein but has no effect on body growth of larvae, with animals reaching a normal final weight setpoint. Notum growth is similar to controls. This demonstrates that ds is not required in the wing to limit body growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B) and weight/growth measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B, D-F). The inference (C97) is well-justified: wing-specific knockdown does not affect body growth, indicating no wing-to-body signaling for growth control.

results.result: The nub>ds(RNAi) wing pouch grows at a faster rate than normal, reaching 28% larger at the WPP stage and 42% larger at the WPP+1 stage. Knockdown of Ds causes the entire allometric relationship to shift such that wings are consistently bigger for their given body size, indicating that Ds is required to tune down the allometric relationship of the wing to the body.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 are supported by volume measurements (Figure 5B-C) and allometric growth data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C). The shift in the entire allometric relationship provides strong evidence for Ds tuning the wing-to-body scaling. The inference (C102) is well-supported.

results.result: Knockdown of Fat-GFP in the wing pouch results in virtually complete elimination of Fat-GFP expression (<5% remaining). This has a weak effect during mid third instar but results in 15% larger wing pouches by WPP stage and 42% larger by WPP+1 stage, comparable to ds(RNAi). Adult wings are 40% larger than controls. Fat and Ds are autonomously required to inhibit wing pouch growth during mid-to-late third instar and its transition to the pupal stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C109 are supported by fluorescence measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D, 3A), volume measurements (Figure 5D-E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2G-H), and adult wing measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I). The inference about autonomous requirement (C109) is well-justified by the wing-specific RNAi experiments.

results.result: Knockdown of ds in the dorsal compartment increases the D/V ratio of compartment size by 60%, but overall wing pouch size is unaffected. This is explained by mechanisms in which compartments sense overall pouch size, resulting in undergrowth of one compartment when there is overgrowth in the other.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 are supported by compartment size measurements in Figures 5G-H. The explanation (C112) is supported by citation to previous work (Diaz-Benjumea and Cohen, 1993) and provides a reasonable interpretation of the compensatory growth phenomenon.

results.result: Compartment-specific knockdown of ds and fat in the posterior compartment increases the P/A ratio by 63% and 23%, respectively, with double knockdown showing a synergistic effect (193% increase). Overall wing pouch size is affected to a lesser extent (10%, 19%, and 32% increases). Fat and Ds have autonomous effects on wing pouch growth consistent with mutant phenotypes, but the autonomous RNAi phenotypes are less severe than whole-body loss, suggesting additional non-autonomous requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C118 are supported by compartment size measurements in Figures 5L-M. The synergistic effect of double knockdown (C115) is particularly notable. The inference about non-autonomous requirements (C118) is reasonable given the difference in severity between RNAi and mutant phenotypes, though this requires further investigation.

results.result: The number of ds(RNAi) cells in the D compartment is 42% higher than wildtype control, while average cell size (apical domain area) is unchanged. The enhanced size of ds(RNAi) wing pouches is primarily driven by an increase in cell number.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 are supported by cell counting and cell size measurements in Figures 5I-J. The inference (C121) is well-justified by the data showing increased cell number without change in cell size. This establishes that Ds regulates growth through cell proliferation rather than cell size.

results.result: The average time for third instar larval wing pouch cells to transit M phase is 20.5 min (0.34 hr), highly similar to previous measurements. The average cell cycle time linearly scales with wing pouch volume during the mid-to-late third instar, with a scaling coefficient predicting that cell cycle length increases 16 hr as wing pouch volume increases by 1 nL.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C126 are supported by live imaging data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and cell cycle time measurements (Figure 6A). The linear scaling relationship is clearly demonstrated, and the scaling coefficient is quantitatively determined. The consistency with previous measurements (C124) strengthens confidence in the methodology.

results.result: The nub>ds(RNAi) cell cycle time linearly scales with wing pouch volume, but the scaling coefficient is much smaller than wildtype (p=6.2×10⁻⁴). This means cell cycle duration does not lengthen as rapidly as normal, resulting in consistently shorter cell cycle times.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129 are supported by cell cycle time measurements in Figure 6B and statistical comparison of linear regression slopes. The p-value indicates a highly significant difference in scaling coefficients. The inference (C129) logically follows from the smaller scaling coefficient.

results.result: The scaling coefficient for nub>fat-GFP(RNAi) cells is much smaller than wildtype (p=3.1×10⁻⁴).
results.evaluation: Claim C130 is supported by statistical comparison of linear regression slopes. The p-value indicates a highly significant difference, consistent with the ds(RNAi) results and supporting a common mechanism for Fat and Ds in regulating cell cycle scaling.

results.result: Model predictions of wing pouch growth are very close to observed pouch growth for wildtype wings and wings with Fat or Ds knocked down by RNAi. This agreement indicates that during the mid-to-late third instar, cell cycle control primarily accounts for wing pouch growth, and the effects of Fat/Ds on wing pouch growth are primarily exerted by their regulation of cell cycle dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 are supported by comparison of model simulations with experimental data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2. The close agreement between model predictions (based solely on cell cycle regulation) and observed growth provides strong evidence that cell cycle control is the primary mechanism. The inferences (C132-C133) are well-justified by this agreement.

results.result: During the third instar, Fat and Ds regulate a mechanism that couples the duration of the cell cycle to overall wing pouch size. They are not essential for the coupling mechanism itself but tune it to ensure the growth rate of the wing is attenuated relative to the body, coordinating the relative scaling of the wing to the final body size.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C136 are summary inferences based on the cell cycle scaling data (C125-C130) and allometric growth data (C42-C45, C92-C94, C99-C102). The inference that Fat and Ds tune rather than create the coupling mechanism (C135) is well-supported by the observation that cell cycle still scales with wing size in RNAi knockdown, but with a different coefficient. The connection to allometric growth (C136) is well-established by the combined data.

results.result: Misexpression of Ds using nub>ds drastically alters the Ds protein gradient and causes changes in the Fat gradient, with the gradient peak skewed to the anterior and not flattening at the WPP stage. However, the growth curve of the third instar wing pouch is indistinguishable from wildtype, and wing growth ceases normally at the WPP stage. This suggests that drastically altering the Ds gradient does not impact wing growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C141 are supported by fluorescence measurements (Figures 7B-C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) and growth measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F-G). The inference (C141) is well-justified: despite dramatic changes in the Ds gradient, growth is normal. This is a critical negative result that challenges the gradient model.

results.result: Overexpression of Ds using ds>Ds strongly amplifies Ds expression while preserving its gradient pattern. The Fat protein gradient resembles wildtype. The wing pouch is approximately 12% larger than wildtype at the WPP stage and in the adult. The scaling coefficient between cell cycle time and wing pouch volume is slightly smaller than wildtype but not significantly (p=0.108). Graded overexpression of Ds only weakly affects growth, and cells appear relatively insensitive to the levels and pattern of Ds expression in terms of their growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C147 are supported by fluorescence measurements (Figures 7D-F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), volume and area measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B-C), and cell cycle measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D). The inferences (C146-C147) are well-supported by the weak growth effect despite strong amplification of Ds expression. This further challenges the gradient model.

results.result: In nub>fat HA animals, both transgenic and endogenous Fat gradients do not diminish in magnitude as larvae approach pupariation and do not flatten at the WPP stage but only at the later WPP+1 stage. However, the relationship between cell cycle time and wing pouch size is indistinguishable from wildtype, and final wing pouch size is normal. Fat and Ds gradient dynamics do not appear to play a significant role in wing growth control.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C152 are supported by fluorescence measurements (Figures 7H-I), cell cycle time measurements (Figure 7J), and volume measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B). The inference (C152) is well-justified: despite altered Fat gradient dynamics, growth and cell cycle regulation are normal. This is a critical result that strongly challenges the gradient model and represents a major conclusion of the paper.

results.result: Fat and Ds attenuate the rate of third instar wing growth so that it properly scales with body growth via a complex allosteric relationship. They do so by tuning the rate at which the cell cycle progressively lengthens in a linear fashion as the third instar wing grows in size, with this rate of lengthening enhanced by the actions of Fat and Ds.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C154 are summary statements based on the allometric growth data (C42-C45, C92-C94, C99-C102) and cell cycle scaling data (C125-C136). These represent the main conclusions of the paper and are well-supported by the combined evidence from multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: It is possible that local Ds-Fat signaling between third instar wing cells attenuates their sensitivity to Dpp as a mitogen, which would require a larger temporal increase in Dpp concentration to trigger cells to divide. This model is consistent with the observation that third instar wing cells do not lengthen their cell cycle as rapidly as normal when Fat or Ds are knocked down.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C167 represent a speculative mechanistic hypothesis connecting Ds-Fat signaling to Dpp sensitivity. While the hypothesis is consistent with the experimental observations (C167) and supported by citations to previous work showing interactions between Fat/Ds and Dpp signaling, it remains speculative without direct experimental evidence. The model is plausible but requires further testing.

results.result: Ds-Fat signaling via the Hippo pathway may regulate the cell cycle duration of wing pouch cells independent of Dpp.
results.evaluation: Claim C170 is a speculative hypothesis based on cited literature suggesting Fat and Dpp may act in parallel. While this is a reasonable alternative to the Dpp-dependent model (C165-C167), there is no direct experimental evidence in this manuscript to support or refute this hypothesis. Further experiments are needed to distinguish between these mechanisms.

results.result: Analysis of Fat/Ds function during the mid-to-late third instar suggests they are not working through the feedforward recruitment mechanism to any large extent. Model simulations of wing pouch growth assuming Fat/Ds only control cell cycle duration strongly fit with measurements of pouch growth during the third instar, arguing that any contribution of Fat/Ds towards recruitment of pouch cells must be minor at this stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C175 are supported by model simulations in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing strong agreement between predictions based solely on cell cycle control and observed growth. The inference that feedforward recruitment is minor during this stage is well-justified by the modeling results, though it does not rule out a role for this mechanism at earlier developmental stages.

results.result: The Ds expression pattern has a graded distribution with a steep slope in the proximal region (near the pouch border) and a shallow slope in the distal region (near the pouch center). Fat protein is distributed in a complementary gradient, most abundant where Ds levels are minimal. Global loss of Ds affects Fat distribution such that Fat is abnormally elevated near the pouch border while remaining unchanged at the pouch center, making a more shallow Fat gradient.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C178 are summary statements of the Ds and Fat gradient observations (C50-C60, C67-C69). These are well-supported by the fluorescence measurements in Figure 2 and provide important descriptive characterization of the protein distributions.

results.result: Cells might repress Fat expression if they sense a steep Ds gradient or in a manner dependent on Ds levels. However, ectopically increasing Ds expression in central regions or amplifying the Ds gradient did not affect Fat abundance as predicted. The distribution of Fat is insensitive to the absolute level or differential in Ds abundance above some minimal non-zero level, below which Fat is upregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C180 are speculative interpretations of the ds mutant results (C178). Claims C182-C183 provide experimental evidence from Ds manipulation experiments that challenge these interpretations. The inference (C184-C185) is well-supported by the combined data: Fat distribution is insensitive to Ds levels above a threshold but responds to loss of Ds. This represents a nuanced understanding of the Fat-Ds interaction.

results.result: It is tempting to speculate that heterophilic binding of Ds to Fat, either in trans or in cis, is responsible for Fat distribution regulation. If so, it is likely distinct from the stabilizing interactions that Ds has on Fat at cell junctions.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C187 are speculative hypotheses based on cited literature about Ds-Fat binding. While the speculation is reasonable given the observed effects of Ds on Fat distribution, there is no direct experimental evidence in this manuscript to test this mechanism. The distinction from junctional stabilization (C187) is a reasonable inference but remains speculative.

results.result: The graded distributions of Fat and Ds proteins across the pouch become progressively more shallow as the larva-pupa transition is reached. For Ds, its gradient scales with the size of the wing pouch because the maximum and minimum limits of Ds-GFP abundance are conserved as the wing pouch grows. This would imply that dividing cells take up intermediate scalar values from their neighbors during growth, and such a mechanism would explain why the Ds gradient scales with pouch volume and not cell number.
results.evaluation: Claim C188 is a summary of gradient dynamics observations (C53, C58). Claim C189 is an inference based on normalized gradient data (C54-C55) and is well-supported. Claims C190-C191 are speculative mechanistic explanations for the gradient scaling. While the speculation is reasonable and consistent with the volume-scaling observations (C76, C81-C82), it remains a hypothesis without direct experimental evidence for the proposed mechanism of cells adopting intermediate values from neighbors.

results.result: The observation of shallowing gradients of Fat and Ds expression fits with a long-standing gradient model for growth regulation. According to this model, a steep gradient of Ds inactivates Fat signaling (stimulates growth), whereas a shallow gradient activates Fat signaling (inhibits growth). A progressively shallowing gradient of Ds would progressively slow down growth, which is what occurs during the third instar. A shallowing gradient of Fat might also fit within this gradient model.
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C196 describe the gradient model from previous work (C193-C194) and note that the observed gradient dynamics (C195) appear consistent with this model. The speculation about Fat gradient fitting the model (C196) is reasonable. However, this apparent consistency is later contradicted by the gradient manipulation experiments (C197-C200), making this a case where initial observations appear to support a model that is ultimately refuted.

results.result: When Fat or Ds protein graded distributions in the wing pouch were manipulated, there was little or no effect on wing growth. Enhancing the gradient of Fat by overexpression did not stimulate growth, and amplifying the Ds gradient by severalfold overexpression led to only a weak growth response. These results are not consistent with the gradient model.
results.evaluation: Claims C197-C200 are supported by the gradient manipulation experiments (C137-C152). The inference (C200) is well-justified: the gradient model predicts that manipulating gradients should have strong effects on growth, but the experiments show little or no effect. This represents a major conclusion that challenges a long-standing model in the field.

results.result: Loss of Fat and Ds diminishes the scaling coefficient that couples cell cycle time to pouch size, and this effect is constant over 36 hr of third instar growth. Ds and Fat are not progressively tuning their impact on growth rate of the wing, as the gradient model predicts. Instead, third instar wing cells are tolerant of differences in Fat/Ds abundance, and the gradients may be linked to the planar cell polarity functions of these proteins.
results.evaluation: Claim C201 is supported by cell cycle time data in Figure 6. The inference (C202) is well-justified: a constant effect over time contradicts the gradient model's prediction of progressive tuning. The inference about tolerance to Fat/Ds abundance differences (C203) is supported by the gradient manipulation experiments (C197-C200). The speculation about planar cell polarity (C204) is reasonable given the citation to previous work, though it remains speculative without direct experimental evidence.

results.result: The authors developed a novel volumetric measurement approach to characterize larval body weight and wing pouch growth dynamics during third instar development. They found that larval body weight increased linearly from 3.0 to 4.0 days AEL, then plateaued, while wing pouch volume increased linearly and continued growing during the non-feeding stage, ceasing at the WPP stage.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised this as a 'novel approach to measure imaginal disc growth' and noted the 'presentation and detail of the presented data is new.' The editor described it as providing 'compelling' evidence, indicating acceptance of these methodological and observational claims.

results.result: The authors characterized allometric growth of the wing pouch relative to body weight, finding two phases of positive allometry with an inflection point when larvae ceased feeding. In fat and ds mutants, allometric growth was significantly altered, with the first phase more extended and the second phase less extended than normal.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the 'more careful analysis of disc volume, larval size, and the relationship between the two' and noted the findings on allometric growth as part of the novel contributions. No concerns were raised about these allometric growth characterizations.

results.result: The authors characterized the Ds-GFP protein gradient across the wing pouch, finding it was graded along both AP and DV axes (high at border, low at center), became progressively shallower as the pouch grew, and scaled with wing pouch volume rather than cell number or area.
results.evaluation: Reviewers identified 'the scaling of gradients of Fat and Ds protein during development' as among 'the most novel results.' The detailed characterization of Ds gradient dynamics and volume-scaling was explicitly recognized as a new contribution without methodological concerns.

results.result: The authors discovered a previously unreported Fat protein gradient that was opposite to the Ds gradient (low at border, high at center), became progressively shallower during development, and was generated by a post-transcriptional mechanism despite uniform fat gene transcription.
results.evaluation: Reviewers specifically highlighted 'a largely unstudied gradient of Fat protein' as one of the most novel results. One reviewer explicitly noted the authors 'observed a previously unreported gradient of Fat protein across the wing blade,' indicating acceptance of this discovery.

results.result: The authors characterized growth phenotypes in fat and ds loss-of-function mutants, finding that both delayed the larva-pupa transition and caused wing disc overgrowth, with fat mutants showing faster growth rates and ds mutants showing extended growth periods.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted these findings were 'consistent with their known role in regulating Hippo pathway activity' and acknowledged the detailed analysis of mutant phenotypes. While not entirely surprising given previous work, the detailed characterization was accepted as part of the comprehensive analysis.

results.result: The authors used tissue-specific RNAi knockdown to demonstrate that Fat and Ds are autonomously required in the wing pouch to inhibit growth during mid-to-late third instar, with knockdown resulting in 28-42% larger wing pouches and altered allometric relationships.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the 'localized knockdown or overexpression of Fat and Ds' as part of the comprehensive experimental approach. The autonomous growth control findings were accepted as consistent with known Fat/Ds functions, with no methodological concerns raised.

results.result: The authors discovered that cell cycle duration increases linearly in direct proportion to wing pouch size during third instar, leading to linear-like growth. Fat/Ds signaling enhances the rate of this cell cycle lengthening, as evidenced by reduced scaling coefficients in RNAi knockdown conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly noted the authors 'show that during mid to late third instar the wing imaginal disc normally grows in a linear rather than exponential fashion and that this occurs due to slowing of the mitotic cell cycle as the disc grows.' This was recognized as a key finding with compelling evidence.

results.result: The authors developed a mathematical model showing that cell cycle control primarily accounts for wing pouch growth during mid-to-late third instar, with Fat/Ds tuning (but not being essential for) the mechanism that couples cell cycle duration to wing size, thereby coordinating allometric scaling.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted the model predictions were 'very close to the observed pouch growth' and accepted the conclusion that 'cell cycle control primarily accounts for wing pouch growth.' The modeling approach and its agreement with experimental data were implicitly accepted without critique.

results.result: The authors tested the functional significance of Fat and Ds gradients by manipulating their expression patterns (nub>ds, ds>Ds overexpression), finding that drastically altering gradients had little or no effect on wing growth, suggesting cells are relatively insensitive to gradient levels and patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers specifically highlighted 'using overexpression of Ds to argue that changes in the Ds gradient do not underlie the slowing and halting of cell divisions during development' as a novel result. One reviewer noted 'graded expression of Fat or Dachsous is not necessary for proper growth regulation in the late third instar,' indicating acceptance of this conclusion.

results.result: The authors tested Fat gradient function by overexpression (nub>fat HA), finding that despite preventing normal gradient flattening at WPP, cell cycle scaling and final wing size remained normal, further supporting that gradient dynamics do not play a significant role in growth control.
results.evaluation: This finding complements the Ds manipulation experiments that reviewers explicitly recognized. The conclusion that 'graded expression of Fat or Dachsous is not necessary for proper growth regulation' encompasses both the Ds and Fat manipulation results, indicating reviewer acceptance.

results.result: The authors demonstrated that Ds and Fat gradient dynamics are coupled to wing pouch volume rather than cell number or area, using trol(RNAi) to alter tissue geometry and en>RBF to alter cell size/number while maintaining compartment size.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the detailed analysis of gradient scaling and its relationship to tissue size. These experiments support the volume-scaling conclusion that was part of the novel gradient characterization findings explicitly recognized by reviewers.

results.result: The authors determined that enhanced wing pouch size in ds(RNAi) animals is primarily driven by increased cell number (42% more cells) rather than changes in cell size.
results.evaluation: This cellular mechanism underlying the growth phenotype was part of the comprehensive analysis of Fat/Ds function. Reviewers accepted the overall growth control findings without raising concerns about the cellular basis.

results.result: The authors found that in ds mutants, Fat protein distribution is altered with abnormally elevated levels near the pouch border while remaining unchanged at the center, and the Fat gradient fails to flatten normally at WPP.
results.evaluation: This observation of Fat gradient changes in ds mutants supports the relationship between Ds and Fat distribution. Reviewers accepted the gradient characterization findings without raising concerns about these mutant phenotypes.

results.result: The authors tested whether Four-jointed (Fj) regulates Fat or Ds distribution, finding that fj mutants showed unchanged Fat and Ds levels and normal wing pouch volume.
results.evaluation: This negative result helps define the mechanism of Fat gradient formation. While not highlighted by reviewers, it was part of the accepted comprehensive characterization of gradient regulation.

results.result: The authors used compartment-specific RNAi (ap>ds, en>ds, en>fat, en>fat ds) to demonstrate autonomous effects on growth, with synergistic effects in double knockdown, though phenotypes were less severe than whole-body mutants, suggesting possible non-autonomous requirements.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the 'localized knockdown' experiments as part of the comprehensive analysis. The autonomous growth control findings and the observation of less severe phenotypes than mutants were accepted without methodological concerns.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate growth measurement methodology and temporal dynamics (C25-C28). OpenEval focuses on these specific claims, while peer review groups them with volumetric claims (C29-C31) and praises the novel measurement approach broadly.

OpenEval evaluates volumetric measurements (C29-C31) separately, while peer review combines these with temporal growth claims (C25-C28) in a single evaluation praising the comprehensive growth measurement approach.

Both address allometric growth patterns (C42-C43). OpenEval includes additional claims (C44-C45) about biphasic patterns and multiple control mechanisms. Peer review also includes mutant allometric data (C92-C93) in the same evaluation.
OpenEval evaluates altered allometric relationships in mutants (C92-C94) separately. Peer review groups these with wild-type allometric growth (C42-C43) as part of the comprehensive analysis.

Both evaluate Ds gradient scaling along AP axis (C50-C55). OpenEval focuses on these specific gradient characterization claims. Peer review also includes volume-scaling claims (C71, C81) in recognizing gradient scaling as a novel result.

Both evaluate volume-scaling experiments with trol(RNAi) (C73-C77). OpenEval and peer review both support these findings. Peer review also includes the complementary cell number manipulation (C78-C83) in the same evaluation.

Both evaluate cell number manipulation experiments (C78-C83). OpenEval treats this separately from trol(RNAi), while peer review groups both volume-scaling experiments together as supporting gradient scaling to tissue size.

Both evaluate Fat gradient characterization (C56-C60). OpenEval focuses on gradient properties and dynamics. Peer review also includes post-transcriptional regulation claims (C61-C63) and summary statement (C177) in recognizing the Fat gradient as a novel discovery.
OpenEval evaluates post-transcriptional regulation of Fat (C61-C63) separately. Peer review groups this with Fat gradient characterization (C56-C60) as part of the novel Fat gradient discovery.

Both evaluate fat mutant phenotypes (C84-C87). OpenEval treats fat and ds mutants separately. Peer review groups both mutant phenotypes (C84-C91) together as consistent with known Hippo pathway roles.
Both evaluate ds mutant phenotypes (C88-C91). OpenEval emphasizes distinct mechanisms from fat mutants. Peer review groups with fat mutant data (C84-C87) as part of comprehensive mutant analysis.

Both evaluate wing-specific Ds knockdown and allometric effects (C99-C102). OpenEval focuses on these specific claims. Peer review also includes autonomous requirement claims (C106-C109) in acknowledging localized manipulation experiments.

Both evaluate autonomous growth control by Fat/Ds (C106-C109). OpenEval includes additional claims (C103-C105) about Fat knockdown. Peer review groups with allometric scaling claims (C99-C102) as part of localized manipulation experiments.

Both evaluate cell cycle scaling with wing size (C125-C126). OpenEval focuses on establishing the linear relationship. Peer review groups with broader claims (C3-C4, C127-C130) about linear growth and cell cycle slowing as a key finding.

Both evaluate altered cell cycle scaling in ds(RNAi) (C127-C129). OpenEval treats this separately from wild-type. Peer review groups with wild-type cell cycle data (C3-C4, C125-C126, C130) as part of the comprehensive cell cycle analysis.
OpenEval evaluates fat(RNAi) cell cycle scaling (C130) separately. Peer review groups this with all cell cycle scaling data (C3-C4, C125-C129) in recognizing the key finding about cell cycle control.

Both evaluate model predictions based on cell cycle control (C131-C133). OpenEval focuses on model-data agreement. Peer review also includes mechanistic interpretation claims (C134-C136) in accepting the modeling approach.

Both evaluate the conclusion that Fat/Ds tune cell cycle coupling (C134-C136). OpenEval treats this as summary inference. Peer review groups with model predictions (C131-C133) in accepting cell cycle control as primary mechanism.

Both evaluate Ds overexpression experiments showing normal growth despite altered gradients (C137-C141). OpenEval and peer review both support this as challenging the gradient model. Peer review also includes Ds amplification data (C142-C147).
